  Abstract
  Background: Injuries to the hamstring muscles are among the most common in sports and account for significant
  time loss. Despite being so common, the injury mechanism of hamstring injuries remains to be determined.
  Purpose: To investigate the hamstring injury mechanism by conducting a systematic review.
  Study design: A systematic review following the PRISMA statement.
  Methods: A systematic search was conducted using PubMed, EMBASE and the Cochrane Library. Studies 1) written
  in English and 2) deciding on the mechanism of hamstring injury were eligible for inclusion. Literature reviews,
  systematic reviews, meta-analyses, conference abstracts, book chapters and editorials were excluded, as well as
  studies where the full text could not be obtained.
  Results: Twenty-six of 2372 screened original studies were included and stratified to the mechanism or
  methods used to determine hamstring injury: stretch-related injuries, kinematic analysis, electromyography-based
  kinematic analysis and strength-related injuries. All studies that reported the stretch-type injury mechanism
  concluded that injury occurs due to extensive hip flexion with a hyperextended knee. The vast majority of
  studies on injuries during running proposed that these injuries occur during the late swing phase of the
  running gait cycle.
  Conclusion: A stretch-type injury to the hamstrings is caused by extensive hip flexion with an extended
  knee. Hamstring injuries during sprinting are most likely to occur due to excessive muscle strain caused by
  eccentric contraction during the late swing phase of the running gait cycle.
  Level of evidence: Level IV
  Keywords: Running, Sprinting, Biomechanics, Strength, Muscle injury

input.command:
cd /Users/kristinarash/Library/Caches/sportsci-batch-100 && python3 - <<'EOF'
import json
d=json.load(open('drafts/Q20.json'))
p=d['paper']
d['evidenceSummary']="A PRISMA systematic review of 26 original studies (from 2,841 screened after removing duplicates) on how hamstring injuries occur, drawing on retrospective injury reports, kinematic studies, kinematic studies with EMG and strength studies, with 444 participant entries across studies (some individuals in more than one study). The authors conclude that stretch-type injuries follow extensive hip flexion with an extended knee, and that sprint-related injuries most likely result from eccentric strain in the late swing phase."
p['findings']="Three stretch-type studies (dancers and water skiers, 12 to 30 subjects each) all reported injury with extensive hip flexion and a hyperextended knee. Of 10 kinematic studies, seven reported the swing phase (late or terminal swing proposed as highest risk), two stance phase and one both phases. Of 10 kinematic-EMG studies, five reported swing phase, one stance phase, two both phases and two other tasks, and three strength studies in football players gave inconclusive results. Three studies recorded an actual injury in real time, and two of these concerned the same subject. The median quality score was 8 (range 7 to 14) of 20."
p['limitations']="The abstract reports 2,372 screened studies, while the Results report 2,841 screened after 1,423 duplicates were removed from 4,264 identified; the Results figure is used here. Table 2 lists 9 kinematic-EMG studies while the text describes 10. Most conclusions are estimates from uninjured participants, and the injury-recording evidence is limited to three case reports. Conditions varied, with some treadmill studies at slow speeds and no studies on grass, quality was low, and the inclusion criterion depended on the authors' own extrapolation."
p['practicalImplications']="Treat late-swing eccentric loading as a working hypothesis for sprint hamstring injury, and for kicking or dance-type movements check for the combination of hip flexion with a straight knee. The review does not test any prevention or training intervention, so it cannot show which exercises reduce injury."
p['rtp']="The review describes how injuries happen, not how to rehabilitate them. The authors suggest that knowledge of forward trunk lean and hip and core control could inform prevention and rehabilitation programmes, but the review gives no return-to-sport criteria or timelines."
d['verification']={"status":"CORRECTED","changes":[
 "evidenceSummary/findings: omitted the three strength-related studies (3+10+10+3=26) -> added ('Three studies investigated hamstring strength in football players'; 'There are inconclusive results')",
 "paper.findings: 'seven reported late swing phase' -> seven reported swing phase, late swing proposed as highest risk ('seven studies concluded that hamstring injuries occur during the swing phase')",
 "paper.limitations: said the 'methods figure' was used -> Results figure; added Table 2 vs text count conflict (Table 2 'Kinematics with electromyographic analysis 9' vs 'Ten studies performed EMG-based kinematic analysis'); 'few studies on grass' -> none ('there is a lack of studies examining the injury mechanism in those conditions')",
 "paper.rtp: attributed hip and core strengthening to the stretch-type findings -> tied to forward trunk lean ('The forward trunk lean can be caused by poor activation and control of the muscles of the core and hip')",
 "paper.practicalImplications: removed eccentric-work and monitoring advice the review does not test"],
 "residualConcerns":"","spotCheckPriority":"high"}
open('verified/Q20.json','w').write(json.dumps(d,indent=1,ensure_ascii=False)+"\n")
EOF
echo ok
